facts.value: The family, a fundamental institution found worldwide, showcases diverse structures and arrangements across cultures. Scholars in sociology and anthropology have recognized a range of family types across various cultural settings. These classifications often depend on factors like organization (nuclear or joint), marriage forms (monogamous or polygamous), authority dynamics (matriarchal or patriarchal), and residence patterns.

Nuclear Family: The nuclear family stands as a foundational unit comprising a husband, wife, and their unmarried children. Prevalent in modern industrialized societies, this familial structure emphasizes the close relationships between parents and offspring. It centers on the spousal relationship, guaranteeing children receive ample care, nurturing, and emotional support.
Joint Family: Joint families are characterized by multiple generations living together under one roof. They often share communal spaces and pool financial resources.
Extended Family: Extended families consist of a wide range of blood relatives, including parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, and their spouses.
Patriarchal Family: The patriarchal family system is distinguished by the centralization of power within the paternal lineage.
Matriarchal Family: The matriarchal family constitutes a domestic arrangement where the primary authority rests with the wife or mother figure.
Patrilocal Family: When the wife relocates to live with the husband’s family.
Matrilocal Family: Matrilocal residence refers to a living arrangement in which a married couple chooses to reside with the wife’s family.
Neolocal Residence: When a married couple decides to establish a new and independent residence after marriage.
Avunculocal Family: In this family arrangement, the newly married couple relocates to the residence of the maternal uncle.
Matri-Patri Local Family: In a matri-patrilocal family, the groom relocates to the bride’s residence immediately after marriage.
Patrilineal Family: In a patrilineal family structure, lineage is traced through the father.
Matrilineal Family: In matrilineal societies, lineage is followed through the female side.
Monogamous Family: A monogamous family consists of one husband and one wife.
Polygamous Family: Polygamous family occurs when one man is married to multiple women, or one woman is married to multiple men.
Polygynous Family: It represents a familial structure where a man maintains marital relationships with multiple wives.
Polyandrous Family: In this family structure, a woman is married to multiple husbands simultaneously.
Endogamous Family: The custom of marrying someone within the same group to which an individual belongs.
Exogamous Family: Involves marriage with someone outside the group.
Consanguine Family: The consanguine family is structured around the parent-child relationship, emphasizing blood descent.
Conjugal Family: The conjugal family is centered around the core unit of the husband, the wife, and their children.
